WAL-CLM-LETS-000317.claim_text: Infarction is the death of an area of tissue because its blood supply was cut off by a plug or thrombus (a blood clot, or a clump of tumor or bacterial cells); in vital areas of the heart or brain a stroke or heart attack can be fatal, and Wallach stresses prevention is always better than trying to repair after the fact. If clumps of bacteria are involved (as in rheumatic fever), antibiotics (penicillin or tetracycline) are required.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000323.claim_text: Irritable bowel syndrome alternates between constipation and diarrhea; Wallach holds that food allergies are the most frequent cause, producing celiac-like small-intestine damage (edema, ulceration, catarrhal inflammation), and that the orthodox approach (low-fiber diets, cortisone, Tagamet) is wrong — a pulse test is extremely useful for finding the individual cause. WAL-CLM-LETS-000325.claim_text: Jaundice (icterus, yellow eyes) can be caused by blockage of the bile-duct system in the liver (gallstones, tumor, hepatitis) and/or destruction of red blood cells (Rh factor, blood parasites, malaria); diagnosis is critical. Examining the whites of the eyes (sclera) reveals true jaundice by a yellow coloration — which is absent when the skin is yellow from high beta-carotene intake; blood tests differentiate obstruction (bilirubin above 2.0-2.5 milligrams percent) from red-blood-cell destruction. Treatment: exposure to ultraviolet light to speed elimination; a liver flush (three days of apple juice, then a cup of olive oil and a cup of lemon juice); vitamin C to bowel tolerance; vitamin A at 300,000 international units per day as beta carotene; selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day; vitamin E at 800-1,200 international units per day; and herbs licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra), agrimony (Agrimonia eupatoria), celandine (Chelidonium majus), and chionanthus (Chionanthus virginica).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000328.claim_text: Keratomalacia (xerophthalmia) is a hazy, dry cornea (the clear domed bulge at the front of the eye) that becomes ulcerated — a sign of vitamin A deficiency. Symptoms include extreme dryness of the eyes with blinking to keep them moist, conjunctivitis, night blindness, and fat-like spots (Bitot's spots) on the white of the eyeball; untreated, it can cause permanent blindness. Treatment: vitamin A at 25,000 international units (children) to 300,000 international units (adults) per day as beta carotene, zinc at 10-50 milligrams three times daily, and increasing animal protein to 120 grams per day (chicken, fish, eggs, milk, lamb, pork, or beef), plus the baseline nutritional program.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000330.claim_text: Kernicterus is the deposition of bile pigments into the brain of a newborn after a prolonged elevation of bilirubin (bile pigments produced from red-blood-cell breakdown); its symptoms mimic cerebral palsy — lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, incoordination, seizures, and death. Prevention and treatment: frequent feeding of the infant to reduce absorption of bile pigments, and exposure to blue and ultraviolet light to photo-oxidize the bilirubin (a transient lactose intolerance can accompany light therapy in infants, causing diarrhea, but this does not appear to have any permanent consequences).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000331.claim_text: Ketoacidosis (ketosis) results from a low glucose supply to the liver, which forces it to metabolize fat — producing 'ketone bodies' (acetoacetic acid, beta-hydroxybutyric acid, and acetone). It occurs in diabetes, alcoholism, hypoglycemia, and starvation. Signs include acetone-smelling breath, nausea and vomiting, air hunger, confusion or coma, extreme thirst, and weight loss; a positive urine 'dipstick' for ketone bodies confirms it. Treatment: resolve the basic disease process (diabetes, hypoglycemia, alcoholism, starvation), increase complex-carbohydrate intake, chromium at 50-200 micrograms three times daily, and the baseline nutritional program.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000332.claim_text: Kidney disease (kidney stones) can be caused by infections, toxins, nutritional excesses (hypervitaminosis D) and deficiencies (vitamin A, selenium, zinc), and can be secondary to cardiovascular disease or diabetes. Contrary to orthodox belief, Wallach holds that kidney stones are caused by calcium AND magnesium deficiencies — which deplete calcium from the bones, the actual source of stone calcium — not by too much calcium; excess vitamin D (suntanning, fish oil, supplements) alongside a calcium deficiency accelerates the depletion. Check for cadmium toxicity with a hair analysis. Treatment: calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 milligrams per day, reduce phosphorus intake, vitamin A at 25,000-300,000 international units per day as beta carotene, vitamin B-6 at 50 milligrams three times daily, lysine and glutamic acid, and herbs (dandelion, dwarf elder, goldenrod, Java tea, parsley, horsetail, mugwort, cranberry juice). Chelation helps; an acute stone blockage may require morphine for pain and prednisone for three days to reduce ureter inflammation, and a 'lithotripter' (ultrasound) can shatter stones without surgery.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000337.claim_text: Lactase deficiency (cow's-milk sensitivity) is a carbohydrate intolerance caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme needed to break milk sugar (lactose) into glucose and galactose; it is marked by bloating, diarrhea, and violent abdominal cramps after consuming cow's milk and cow's-milk products. Wallach cites prevalences of about 20% in adults of Northwest European origin, 75% in adults of all other ethnic groups, 90% of Orientals, and 75% of Blacks and American Indians, with the ability to digest lactose gradually lost between ages 10 and 20. Treatment: avoid lactose-containing foods and/or predigest the lactose by adding lactase enzyme to milk-containing foods.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000337.verbatim:
Treatment of lactose intolerance includes
avoidance of lactose containing foods and/or
predigestion of lactose by adding lactase to
milk containing foods.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000338.claim_text: Laryngitis (loss of voice) can be caused by bacterial or viral infections and extreme overuse of the vocal cords (e.g., yelling at a football or hockey game); frequently the temperature is not elevated and voice loss is the only symptom. A 'Strep' throat cause can be dangerous and lead to rheumatic fever or meningitis if not treated. Treatment: penicillin or tetracycline for Strep throat at 250 milligrams orally every 6 hours for 10-12 days, voice rest, honey/lemon preparations, and herbs including cajuput (Melaleuca leucadendron), sunflower (Helianthus annuus), pine oils (Pinus sylvestris), black caraway (Pimpinella saxifraga), garden sage (Salvia officinalis), high mallow (Malva sylvestris), wild ginger (Asarum europaeum), and eucalyptus (Eucalyptus globulus). Viral laryngitis may be treated with Isoprinosine at 500-1,500 milligrams per day or Ribavirin at 250-1,500 milligrams per day (pregnant women should avoid these drugs — they are teratogenic in lab animals).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000340.claim_text: Lead poisoning (plumbism) can cause a wide variety of symptoms — learning disabilities, kidney disease, stunted bone growth, headaches, and gastrointestinal disease; often the lead is eaten because of 'pica', a compulsive eating of unusual things driven by mineral deficiencies. Sources include paint chips, window caulking, pottery glaze, lead-arsenate garden sprays, leaded-fuel pollution, smoke from burning batteries, and lead-insulated wire; diagnose via hair analysis (chronic cases) or blood (sudden, acute cases). Treatment: vitamin C to bowel tolerance; chelation with calcium EDTA at 10-25 infusions and/or oral D-penicillamine; and the baseline supplement program with plant-derived colloidal minerals, because chelation depletes the body's mineral stores (selenium is of particular value).

cillamine. Don't forget the base line nutri-
tional supplement program containing plant
derived colloidal minerals because the chela-

minerals ( selenium is of particular value).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000341.claim_text: Legionnaires' disease is caused by infection with Legionella pneumophila; it is characterized by pneumonia, high fever, slow heart rate, dry cough, chills, pleuritis, and diarrhea. A relatively new disease (discovered in 1976), it is fatal in 80% of untreated cases and is diagnosed by growing the organism on charcoal-yeast extract from sputum; immunosuppressed patients (those on chemotherapy, transplant patients, AIDS patients) are most susceptible. Treatment is specific: erythromycin at 500 milligrams to 1 gram orally or intravenously every 6 hours for three weeks.
WAL-CLM-LETS-000341.verbatim:

with erythromycin at 500 mg to 1 gm orally or
IV q 6 H for three weeks.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000342.claim_text: Lentigo-maligna melanoma (a skin cancer) originates from Hutchinson's freckle on sun-exposed areas (face, neck, anus, torso) — large flat tan or brown lesions with darker spots, slow-growing (about ten years to invade the deep skin layers). Treatment can include excision biopsy or complete surgical removal; for facial tumors a cream such as Carcelim (requiring 30 days of application) may be preferable. Wallach also recommends vitamin C to bowel tolerance, vitamin A at 300,000 international units per day as beta carotene, selenium at 1,000 micrograms per day, and a #40 sunscreen to prevent new cancers, plus the baseline nutritional program. WAL-CLM-LETS-000343.claim_text: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease, infectious jaundice) is an infectious disease caused by Leptospira, a spirochete bacterium carried by dogs, rats, and various wild animals; people are infected through urine-contaminated water or cuts while skinning or butchering infected animals. Symptoms include anemia, jaundice, proteinuria, hematuria, and occasionally aseptic meningitis, with fever and chills consistent; diagnosis needs blood tests or urine cultures. Treatment with antibiotics is most effective if started within four days of onset — tetracycline at 500 milligrams four times daily is effective.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000344.claim_text: Leukemia (blood cancer) is a cancer of the blood-forming tissues of the bone marrow; no exact cause is proven, though viruses, radiation, and chemicals such as benzene are implicated. It produces a defect in white-blood-cell maturation, flooding the circulation with immature white cells; diagnosis comes from a blood test showing anemia, low platelets, increased lymphoblasts, and an elevated total white-cell count, and symptoms include weakness, joint pain, anemia, enlarged lymph nodes, and an enlarged spleen. Wallach's treatment includes Laetrile, hydrogen peroxide, intravenous DMSO (said to mature the immature cells), Onco-Tox, shark liver extract, hydrazine sulfate, cesium chloride, polyerga, germanium, carbamide, and as needed micro-dose chemotherapy, intravenous amino acids, vitamin C to bowel tolerance, selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day, and vitamin A at 300,000 international units as beta carotene. (Captured for the search corpus as deep-dive cancer content with several controversial alternative agents; foundational coverage already exists via the essentials and deficiency claims.)

WAL-CLM-LETS-000345.claim_text: Leukorrhea (vaginal discharge) is a nonspecific vaginal discharge containing mucus and white blood cells, occasionally blood-tinged; it can be caused by Candida albicans, Hemophilus vaginalis, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus (the organism behind toxic-shock syndrome with incorrectly used tampons), or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Specific diagnosis requires culture and/or microscopy of the discharge. Treatment targets the causative organism: vaginal triple-sulfonamide creams, oxytetracycline vaginal suppositories, vinegar douches (30 milliliters per pint of water), and 1.5% hydrogen peroxide (as Oxy-Toddy); gonorrhea also requires systemic antibiotics. Wallach notes that any venereal disease must be reported to the Public Health Department.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000346.claim_text: Lice (pediculosis) can infest the head (Pediculus humanus capitis), body (P. h. corporis), and pubic area (Phthirius pubis); the eggs (nits) are white, oval, seed-like objects attached to the base of the hairs, and adult lice can be seen scuttling through the hair. Itching and irritated skin are the most common symptoms, and diagnosis depends on finding adult lice or nits. Treatment: a hair wash of Labrador tea (Ledum latifolium) or field larkspur (Delphinium consolida), and a special fine-toothed comb to 'harvest' the nits, done daily for fourteen days to break the lice life cycle. For stubborn cases, 1% gamma benzene hexachloride as a shampoo daily for two days, reapplied in ten days (avoid prolonged use, as it can cause genital skin irritation, especially in males).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000347.claim_text: Wallach holds that the potential lifespan for humans is 120-130 years, yet insurance actuary tables put the average at only 72 for males and 78 for females — a 40-50 year gap to work toward. He says home water-filtration systems, air filters and conditioners, and the baseline nutrition program can each add years, and that digestive aids (betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes) add another ten — about twenty added years when pursued actively. He attributes the Hunza secret of longevity (averaging 100 years, up to 140) to the daily consumption of plant-derived colloidal minerals, and warns that exercise alone — without attention to food allergies, digestive aids, the baseline program, colloidal minerals, and avoiding pollutants — will only shorten life. He also notes that 40% of hospital patients are there because of iatrogenic (doctor-caused) disease. (Captured for the search corpus as Wallach's general longevity guidance.)

WAL-CLM-LETS-000348.claim_text: For liver disease (cirrhosis and nonviral hepatitis), Wallach says it is diagnosed by blood tests showing elevated liver-function markers (the SGOT, SGPT and GGT enzymes, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin), with elevated urine ketones, jaundice, delayed clotting, a swollen tender liver under the right ribs, dry itchy skin (an essential-fatty-acid problem), anemia (iron-storage and vitamin B-12/folic-acid deficiency), weight loss and ketosis (he adds: also see gallbladder disease). His treatment is chelation with complete intravenous supplementation including amino acids and interlipids; vitamin C to bowel tolerance; vitamin A at 300,000 international units per day as beta carotene; B-complex at 100 milligrams each three times a day; selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day; vitamin B-12 at 1,000 micrograms per day; folic acid at 15-25 milligrams per day; essential fatty acids (both salmon oil and flaxseed oil) at 1 gram three times a day; and herbs including tamarac (Larix americana), parsley (Carum petroselinum), hemp agrimony (Eupatorium cannabinum) and milk thistle (Silybum marianum) — plus the baseline nutrition program and colloidal minerals.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000349.claim_text: For lockjaw (tetanus) — caused by the toxin of Clostridium tetani, a normal inhabitant of animal manure that enters through puncture wounds and paralyzes the voluntary muscles including the jaw (masseter) muscles — Wallach stresses prevention as the best option: make the puncture wound bleed by squeezing it, open small foot or hand punctures to clean with soap and water, then disinfect with 3% hydrogen peroxide, and take cramp bark tea (Viburnum opulus) in tablespoon doses as needed; he says these minimal steps prevent lockjaw almost 100% of the time. Once it develops, treatment requires tetanus-neutralizing (non-fixed) antitoxin, cleaning and disinfecting the infected wound with hydrogen peroxide, penicillin at two million units intravenously every 6 hours OR tetracycline at 500 milligrams intravenously every 6 hours, sedation to control muscle spasms, and intravenous fluids and electrolytes until the patient can eat and drink on their own.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000350.claim_text: For lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) — a connective-tissue disease with 90% of cases in women in their 30s — Wallach argues the autoimmune antibody attack is a result of the disease and its abnormal proteins, not its cause. He notes the classic sudden onset of fever, fatigue, arthritis and joint pain (often misdiagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis), a facial 'butterfly' rash, severe hair loss and papular skin lesions, and recommends the pulse test to find food allergies (wheat, cow's milk and soy are most common). His treatment is: avoid offending food allergens and rotate non-allergic foods; autoimmune urine therapy; chelation with total nutrition for 15-25 infusions; essential fatty acids (salmon oil and flaxseed oil) at 5 grams three times a day; selenium at 500-1,000 micrograms per day; carnitine (printed 'B-carnitine') at 500 milligrams per day; avoid beef, dairy and alfalfa; and daily doses of plant-derived colloidal minerals.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000351.claim_text: For Lyme disease (Lyme arthritis) — a spirochete bacterial infection transmitted by ticks, first described in 1975 in Lyme, Connecticut — Wallach notes that 3 to 32 days after an infected tick bite a skin lesion called erythema chronicum migrans appears on the thigh, buttock or axilla and expands up to 50 cm, with recurring attacks of arthritis, fatigue, chills, fever, stiff neck, sore muscles, nausea and vomiting, and heart involvement (an enlarged heart and atrioventricular [AV] block) in 8% of patients. It occurs most in children who play in grass or deep woods or who have a dog that brings home the Ixodes dammini tick, clusters along the U.S. northeastern coast and in Wisconsin, California and Oregon, and is often misdiagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis. His treatment is tetracycline at 250-500 milligrams four times a day for 20 days; in children, whose teeth tetracyclines discolor, penicillin at 20 million units per day intravenously in divided doses.

WAL-CLM-LETS-000352.claim_text: Wallach defines malnutrition as occurring either as an overt nutritional deficiency, secondary to extended use of medications that interfere with nutrient absorption, or as malabsorption from celiac disease or low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria). He argues conventional doctors think of malnutrition only as protein/calorie deprivation and miss macro- and micro-nutrient deficiencies (singly or in combination, especially early), and miss that celiac changes in the small-intestine lining arise from subclinical allergies to wheat, cow's-milk albumen and soy (and rye, barley, beef, eggs). In his framework many degenerative diseases are really malabsorption: diabetes and hypoglycemia as chromium/vanadium deficiencies, cystic fibrosis as a selenium and essential-fatty-acid deficiency, arthritis as a calcium deficiency worsened by excess dietary phosphorus, and cancer as a depleted immune system run out of repair nutrients. He concludes malnutrition from malabsorption is the common denominator of almost all degenerative disease, and that liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals are the most efficient way to get minerals into malnourished people. (Note: in the book this entry's text is split by the two-column scan order; the reading order is reassembled here.)

WAL-CLM-LETS-000353.claim_text: Measles (rubeola) is a highly contagious viral disease of sudden onset with cough, nasal drainage, conjunctivitis, Koplik's spots (eruptions on the mouth and lip lining), and a pimple-like rash starting on the head and neck and spreading to the body, arms and legs; fever to 104°F is common, and pneumonia and encephalitis are unusual but potentially fatal complications. Wallach notes it now affects mainly teenagers and young adults, incubates 7-14 days (the diagnostic Koplik's spots appear about four days after the fever), and that having had measles confers lifelong immunity. His treatment is topical over-the-counter anti-itch products (for example Caladryl) plus herbs: salves of marigold (Calendula officinalis), and taken orally columbine (Aquilegia vulgaris), yarrow (Achillea millefolium) and pleurisy root (Asclepias tuberosa).

WAL-CLM-LETS-000354.claim_text: German measles (rubella, three-day measles) is a contagious viral disease that causes mild symptoms in children, including swollen lymph nodes of the head and neck; its incubation is 14-21 days and overt symptoms may be absent in teenagers and adults. The typical rash appears first on the face and spreads quickly to the body and limbs with a general flush like scarlet fever; adults may have enlarged head and neck lymph nodes and adult males may have brief testicular pain. Wallach's treatment is the same symptomatic therapy used for ordinary (nine-day) measles. He states emphatically (in capitals) that rubella is a dangerous disease in pregnant women that can induce spontaneous abortions and birth defects, and gives his editorial opinion that rubella vaccines will cause similar birth defects and so should be avoided during pregnancy.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000242.verbatim:
Choline
Fatty liver, kidney hemorrhage, Alzheimer’s disease, tardive dyskinesia, Huntington's disease (treatment requires 20 G per day).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000243.claim_text: Wallach lists the common diseases of bioflavonoid deficiency in Table 11-9: capillary hemorrhage and reduced immune function.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000243.verbatim:
Bioflavonoids - 1936
capillary hemorrhage, reduced immune function.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000244.claim_text: Wallach says silicon (silica) supplementation increases the collagen in growing bone by 100%, and that tissue levels of silicon decrease with age in people and laboratory animals who are not supplemented.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000244.verbatim:
Silicon supplementation increases the
collagen in growing bone by 100 %. Tissue
levels of Si decrease with aging in
unsupplemented humans and laboratory
species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000245.claim_text: Wallach states that silica deficiency is characterized by dry brittle hair, brittle finger and toe nails, poor skin quality, poor calcium utilization, and arterial disease.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000245.verbatim:
Silica deficiency is characterized
by dry brittle hair, brittle finger and toe nails,
poor skin quality, poor calcium utilization
and arterial disease.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000246.claim_text: Wallach notes that high-fiber diets contain a lot of silicon, which leads many investigators to think silicon helps lower cholesterol; he gives a recommended silicon intake of 200 to 500 mg per day.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000246.verbatim:
High fiber diets contain lots of Si which leads many investigators to think that Si helps to lower cholesterol. The recommended intake of Si ranges
from 200 to 500 mg/day.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000247.claim_text: Wallach reports that samarium, a 'light' rare earth, enhances normal cell proliferation and doubles the life span of laboratory species.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000247.verbatim: Samarium enhances normal cell proliferation and doubles the life span of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000248.claim_text: Wallach reports that tin — once dismissed as mere environmental contamination of tissue — was shown by Schwarz's careful studies to accelerate growth in rats and to meet the standards for an essential trace element (formally demonstrated in 1970); as a member of the fourth main chemical group, tin shares chemical and physical properties with carbon, silica, germanium and lead.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000248.verbatim: Originally the presence of tin in tissue was attributed to environmental contamination; however, careful and detailed studies by Schwarz demonstrated that tin produced an acceleration of growth in rats and further met the standards for an essential trace element.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000249.claim_text: Wallach reports that tin exerts a strong induction effect on the enzyme heme oxygenase, enhancing the breakdown of heme in the kidney, and cites evidence that tin has cancer-prevention properties.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000249.verbatim: Tin has been shown to exert a strong induction effect on the enzyme heme oxygenase, enhancing heme breakdown in the kidney. There is also evidence for tin having cancer prevention properties.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000250.claim_text: Wallach distinguishes natural strontium — which can replace calcium in many organisms and shows considerable evidence of essentiality in mammals including humans — from strontium-90, the man-made product of atomic-fission explosions and the great biohazard fear of the Cold War, which does not occur in nature.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000250.verbatim: Strontium 90, the man made product of fission atomic explosions and the greatest biohazard fear during the cold war, does not occur in nature.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000251.claim_text: Wallach reports that thulium, a 'heavy' rare earth, enhances the growth of normal cells and has doubled the life spans of laboratory species.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000251.verbatim: Thulium supplementation enhances the growth of normal cells and has doubled the life spans of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000252.claim_text: Wallach notes that thallium accumulates in the mammalian kidney and is highly toxic to mammals, including humans.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000252.verbatim: land animals at 0.4 ppm (accumulates in the mammalian kidney and is highly toxic to mammals including man).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000253.claim_text: Wallach reports that vanadium was proven an essential trace mineral in 1971, and that its absorption depends heavily on form — metallic vanadium (vanadyl sulfate) is taken up from the intestinal tract very poorly (only 0.1 to 1.0 percent), vanadium chelates at 40 percent, and plant-derived colloidal vanadium at up to 98 percent.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000253.verbatim: Metallic vanadium (vanadyl sulfate) is absorbed from the intestinal tract very poorly at only 0.1 to 1.0 %; vanadium chelates at 40 % and plant derived colloidals at up to 98 %.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000254.claim_text: Wallach reports that vanadium stimulates glucose (blood sugar) oxidation and transport in fat cells and glycogen (animal starch) synthesis in the liver and muscle, while inhibiting liver gluconeogenesis (the production of glucose from fat) and the absorption of glucose from the gut.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000254.verbatim: Vanadium stimulates glucose (blood sugar) oxidation and transport in fat cells and glycogen (animal starch) synthesis in liver and muscle, and inhibits liver gluconeogenisis (production of glucose from fat) and absorption of glucose from the gut.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000255.claim_text: Wallach reports that vanadium initiates an increase in the contractile force of heart muscle, known as the 'inotropic effect.'
WAL-CLM-RARE-000255.verbatim: Vanadium initiates an increase in the contractile force of heart muscle known as the “inotropic effect.”

WAL-CLM-RARE-000256.claim_text: Wallach reports that vanadium inhibits cholesterol synthesis in animals and humans, which is followed by decreased plasma cholesterol levels and reduced aortic cholesterol.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000256.verbatim: Vanadium inhibits cholesterol synthesis in animals and humans; this is followed by decreased plasma levels of cholesterol and reduced aortic cholesterol.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000257.claim_text: Wallach lists the clinical diseases associated with vanadium deficiency: slow growth, increased infant mortality, infertility, elevated cholesterol, elevated triglycerides, hypoglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and obesity.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000257.verbatim:
Clinical diseases associated with Vanadium deficiency include:
Slow growth
Increased infant mortality
Infertility
Elevated cholesterol
Elevated triglycerides
Hypoglycemia
Hyperinsulinemia
Diabetes
Cardiovascular disease
Obesity

WAL-CLM-RARE-000258.claim_text: Wallach notes that xenon binds to mammalian hemoglobin and myoglobin, producing an anesthetic effect.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000258.verbatim: Xenon binds to mammalian hemoglobin and myoglobin producing an anesthetic effect.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000259.claim_text: Wallach reports that yttrium, a 'heavy' rare earth, enhances normal cell growth and doubles the life span of laboratory species.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000259.verbatim: Yttrium enhances normal cell growth and doubles the life span of laboratory species.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000260.claim_text: Wallach reports that yttrium readily crosses the placenta — exposure of pregnant mice to yttrium leads to rapid placental transfer, with 14 percent of ingested yttrium detectable in the newborn mice.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000260.verbatim: Exposure of pregnant mice to yttrium leads to rapid placental transfer, 14% of ingested Y can be detected in newborn mice.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000261.claim_text: Wallach reports that ytterbium readily crosses the placenta — exposure of pregnant mice leads to rapid placental transfer, with 14 percent of ingested ytterbium detectable in the newborn mice.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000261.verbatim: Exposure of pregnant mice leads to rapid placental transfer, 14% of ingested Yb can be detected in newborn mice.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000262.claim_text: Wallach's Table 11-24 lists the congenital birth defects associated with zinc deficiency: Down's Syndrome, cleft lip, cleft palate, brain defects (dorsal herniation, hydroencephalocele), micro- or anophthalmia (small or absent eyes), micro- or agnathia (small or absent jaw), spina bifida, clubbed limbs, syndactyly (webbed toes and fingers), diaphragmatic (hiatal) hernias, umbilical hernias, heart defects, lung defects, and urogenital defects.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000262.verbatim:
Table 11-24. Congenital Birth defects associated with Zinc Deficiency.
Down’s Syndrome
Cleft lip
Cleft palate
Brain defects (dorsal herniation, hydroencephalocele)
Micro- or anophthalmia (small or absent eyes)
Micro- or agnathia
Spina bifida
clubbed limbs
Syndactyly (webbed toes and fingers)
Diaphragmatic hernias (hiatal hernia)
Umbilical hernias
Heart defects
lung defects
Urogenital

WAL-CLM-RARE-000263.claim_text: Wallach's Table 11-25 lists the symptoms and diseases of zinc deficiency (part 1 of 2): pica (the eating of non-food substances — geophagia/earth-eating, wool eating, hair eating), loss of the sense of smell, loss of the sense of taste, infertility, failure of wounds and ulcers to heal, immune-status failure, poor growth (short stature), high infant mortality, hypogonadism (small, poorly functioning ovaries and testes), remaining in a prepuberty state, and anemia.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000263.verbatim:
Table 11-25. Symptoms and Diseases of Zinc Deficiency
Pica (geophagia, wool eating, hair eating, etc.)
Loss of sense of smell
Loss of sense of taste
Infertility
Failure of wounds and ulcers to heal
Immune status failure
Poor growth (short stature)
High infant mortality
Hypogonadism (small poorly functioning ovaries and testes)
Remains in a prepuberty state
Anemia

WAL-CLM-RARE-000264.claim_text: Wallach's Table 11-25 lists the symptoms and diseases of zinc deficiency (part 2 of 2): alopecia (hair loss), acrodermatitis enteropathica (parakeratosis in pigs and calves), 'frizzy' hair, diarrhea, depression, paranoia, oral and perioral dermatitis, weight loss (anorexia nervosa), benign prostatic hypertrophy (prostate enlargement), severe body odor ('smelly tennis shoe' syndrome), and anorexia and bulimia.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000264.verbatim:
Alopecia (hair loss)
Acrodermatitis enteropathica (Parakeratosis in pigs and calves)
“Frizzy” hair
Diarrhea
Depression
Paranoia
Oral and perioral dermatitis
Weight loss (anorexia nervosa)
Benign prostatic hypertrophy (prostate enlargement)
Severe body odor (“smelly tennis shoe” syndrome)
Anorexia & Bulimia

WAL-CLM-RARE-000265.claim_text: Wallach reports that no fewer than 70 metalloenzymes require zinc to function — including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase, and carboxypeptidase. Zinc helps bind enzymes to their substrates by maintaining the correct spatial and configurational relationships, and some enzymes bind zinc so tightly that they keep functioning even during severe zinc depletion. Zinc is also required by the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and thymidine kinase.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000265.verbatim: There are no less than 70 metalloenzymes that require Zn to function, these include carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase and carboxypeptidase. Zinc helps to bind enzymes to substrates by maintaining spatial and configurational relationships. Some enzymes bind Zn so tightly that even during severe Zn depletion they can still function.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000266.claim_text: Wallach reports that the adult human body contains 1.4 to 2.3 grams of zinc, with the greatest reserves in the liver, pancreas, kidney, bone, and skeletal muscles, and lesser amounts in the eye, prostate gland, semen, skin, hair, fingernails, and toenails.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000266.verbatim: There is 1.4 to 2.3 grams of Zn in the adult human. The liver, pancreas, kidney, bone and skeletal muscles have the greatest reserves of Zn, lesser amounts are found in the eye, prostate gland, semen, skin, hair, fingernails and toenails.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000267.claim_text: Wallach notes the late recognition of zinc's essentiality: it was known to be essential for bread mold 100 years ago, for rats 50 years ago, and for humans only 20 years ago.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000267.verbatim: Zinc was known to be essential for bread mold 100 years ago, essential for rats 50 years ago and for humans only 20 years ago.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000268.claim_text: Wallach reports that heavy losses of zinc occur in sweat, so unsupplemented athletes are particularly at risk for zinc deficiency — manifesting as anorexia nervosa, muscle weakness, pica, and similar signs.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000268.verbatim: Heavy losses of Zn occurs in sweat, therefore unsupplemented athletes are particularly at risk for Zn deficiency (i.e.- anorexia nervosa, muscle weakness, pica, etc.).

WAL-CLM-RARE-000269.claim_text: Wallach's Table 11-23 lists the diseases of selenium deficiency (part 1 of 2): HIV/AIDS (human immunodeficiency virus / acquired immunodeficiency syndrome), anemia (red-blood-cell fragility), 'age spots' and 'liver spots,' fatigue, muscular weakness, myalgia (muscle pain and soreness), scoliosis, muscular dystrophy (including white muscle disease and stiff lamb disease), congenital cystic fibrosis, cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease, 'mulberry heart' disease), multiple sclerosis (associated with mercury poisoning), heart palpitations, irregular heartbeat, and liver cirrhosis.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000269.verbatim:
Table 11-23. Selenium Deficiency Diseases.
HIV (AIDS)
Anemia (RBC fragility)
“Age Spots” & “Liver Spots”
Fatigue
Muscular weakness
Myalgia (muscle pain and soreness)
Scoliosis
Muscular Dystrophy (MD, White Muscle Disease, Stiff Lamb Disease)
Cystic Fibrosis (congenital)
Cardiomyopathy (Keshan Disease, “Mulberry heart” Disease)
Multiple Sclerosis (MS) - associated with Hg poisoning
Heart palpitations
Irregular heart beat
Liver cirrhosis

WAL-CLM-RARE-000270.claim_text: Wallach's Table 11-23 lists the diseases of selenium deficiency (part 2 of 2): pancreatitis, pancreatic atrophy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig's disease, associated with mercury poisoning), Parkinson's disease (associated with mercury poisoning), Alzheimer's disease (associated with high vegetable-oil consumption), adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD, 'Lorenzo's Oil' syndrome), infertility, low birth weight, high infant mortality, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), cancer (associated with carcinogen contact and high vegetable-oil intake), clinical AIDS (human immunodeficiency virus infection), and sickle cell anemia.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000270.verbatim:
Pancreatitis
Pancreatic atrophy
Lou Gehrig's Disease (ALS) - associated with Hg poisoning
Parkinson's Disease - associated with Hg poisoning
Alzheimer’s Disease - associated with high vegetable oil consumption
Adrenoleucodystrophy (ALD -"Lorenzo’s Oil’ Syndrome)
Infertility
Low birth weight
High infant mortality
Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)
Cancer - associated with carcinogen contact as well as high vegetable oil intake
Clinical AIDS (HIV infection)
Sickle cell anemia

WAL-CLM-RARE-000271.claim_text: Wallach quotes U.S. Senate Document 264 (1936): the alarming fact is that foods — fruits, vegetables, and grains — now raised on millions of acres of land that no longer contain enough of certain needed minerals are 'starving us,' no matter how much of them we eat.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000271.verbatim: “The alarming fact is that foods - fruits and vegetables and grains, now being raised on millions of acres of land that no longer contains enough of certain needed minerals, are starving us - no matter how much of them we eat! “

WAL-CLM-RARE-000272.claim_text: Wallach quotes U.S. Senate Document 264 (1936): no person today can eat enough fruits and vegetables to supply the stomach with the mineral salts required for perfect health, because the stomach is not big enough to hold them.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000272.verbatim: “No man of today can eat enough fruits and vegetables to supply his stomach with the mineral salts he requires for perfect health, because his stomach isn’t big enough to hold them!”

WAL-CLM-RARE-000273.claim_text: Wallach quotes U.S. Senate Document 264 (1936): leading authorities report that 99% of the American people are deficient in these minerals, and that a marked deficiency in any one of the more important minerals actually results in disease — any considerable lack of an element, however microscopic the body's requirement, makes us sicken, suffer, and shorten our lives.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000273.verbatim: “It is bad news to learn from our leading authorities that 99 % of the American people are deficient in these minerals, and that a marked deficiency in any one of the more important minerals actually results in disease. Any upset of the balance, any considerable lack of one or another element, however microscopic the body requirement might be, and we sicken, suffer, and shorten our lives.”

WAL-CLM-RARE-000274.claim_text: Wallach cites the June 1992 Rio Earth Summit Report on the decline of nutritional minerals in the world's farm and range soils over the last 100 years, by continent: North America (United States, Canada, Mexico) is the most depleted at 85%, followed by Asia and South America at 76%, Africa at 74%, Europe at 72%, and Australia at 55% — giving numerical weight to the 1936 U.S. Senate Document 264 warning.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000274.verbatim:
Minerals
Continent % Depleted over 100 years
Africa 74 %
Asia 76 %
Australia 55 %
Europe 72 %
North America 85 %
South America 76 %

WAL-CLM-RARE-000275.claim_text: Wallach's Table 7-8 maps common degenerative diseases of humans to their causal nutrient deficiencies: osteoporosis and arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis) to calcium, magnesium, boron, copper, and sulfur; hypertension and bone spurs/heel spurs/calcium deposits to calcium, magnesium, and boron; cancer, cardiomyopathy, and cataracts to selenium; diabetes to chromium, vanadium, and zinc; aneurysms to copper; and deafness to tin.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000275.verbatim:
Table 7-8. Common Degenerative Diseases of Humans and Their Cause.
Osteoporosis: Ca, Mg, B, Cu, S
Arthritis (Ankylosing spondylitis): Ca, Mg, B, Cu, S
Hypertension: Ca, Mg, B
Bone spurs, heel spurs, Ca deposits: Ca, Mg, B
Cancer: Se
Diabetes: Cr, Va, Zn
Aneurysms: Cu
Cardiomyopathy: Se
Cataracts: Se
Deafness: Sn

WAL-CLM-RARE-000276.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists tranquilizers and sleeping aids regarded as unsuitable for older patients (part 1 of 2) — Diazepam (Valium), Chlordiazepoxide (Librium), and Flurazepam (Dalmane), all addictive and/or too long-acting and prone to cause falls — with the mineral replacement to address the underlying need instead: calcium, magnesium, lithium, chromium, and vanadium (while avoiding sugar, natural and processed, and caffeine).
WAL-CLM-RARE-000276.verbatim:
Tranquilizers & Sleeping Aids — Mineral Replacement: Ca, Mg, Li, Cr, Va (avoid sugar, natural and processed, and caffeine):
Diazepam (Valium) - Tranquilizer. Addictive and too long-acting, causing drowsiness, confusion and falls.
Chlordiazepoxide (Librium) - Tranquilizer. Too long-acting causes falls.
Flurazepam (Dalmane), a sleeping aid. Too long-acting, causes falls.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000277.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1, tranquilizers/sleeping aids unsuitable for older patients (part 2 of 2) — Meprobamate (Miltown, Deprol, Equagesic, Equanil), Pentobarbital (Nembutal), and Secobarbital (Seconal) — with the same mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, lithium, chromium, and vanadium.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000277.verbatim:
Meprobamate (Miltown, Deprol, Equagesic, Equanil) - Tranquilizer, sometimes combined with an anti-depressant or pain reliever. Addictive, too long-acting, causes falls.
Pentobarbital (Nembutol) - Sedative. Addictive, long-acting, can cause falls.
Secobarbitol (Seconal). Addictive, long acting, causes falls.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000278.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists the antidepressant Amitriptyline (Elavil, Endep, Etrafon, Limbitrol, Triavil) as unsuitable for older patients (stops urination, causes dizziness, drowsiness and falls), with the mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, lithium, chromium, and vanadium.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000278.verbatim:
Antidepressants — Mineral Replacement: Ca, Mg, Li, Cr, Va:
Amitriptyline (Elavil, Endep, Etrafon, Limbitrol, Triavil). Stops the ability to urinate, causes dizziness and drowsiness, causes falls.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000279.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists arthritis drugs unsuitable for older patients — Indomethacin (Indocin; can cause confusion and headaches) and Phenylbutazone (Butazolidin; risk of bone-marrow toxicity) — with the mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, boron, copper, selenium, lithium, plus chondroitin sulfate (Knox gelatin).
WAL-CLM-RARE-000279.verbatim:
Arthritis Drugs — Mineral Replacement: Ca, Mg, B, Cu, Se, Li, chondroitin sulfate (Knox gelatin):
Indomethacin (Indocin). Can cause confusion and headaches.
Phenylbutazone (Butazolidin) - risk of bone marrow toxicity.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000280.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists the diabetes drug Chlorpropamide (Diabinese) as unsuitable for older patients (dangerous fluid retention, slow excretion), with the mineral replacement: chromium, vanadium, and zinc (no sugar).
WAL-CLM-RARE-000280.verbatim:
Diabetes Drugs — Mineral Replacement: Cr, Va, Zn (no sugar, natural or processed):
Chlorpropramide (Diabinase) - Can cause dangerous fluid retention, is excreted slowly; overdose requires long intensive treatment period.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000281.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists pain relievers unsuitable for older patients — Propoxyphene (Darvon Compound, Darvocet, Wygesic) and Pentazocine (Talwin), both addictive, no more effective than aspirin, with more side effects than morphine and risk of seizures and heart complications — with the mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, copper, and selenium.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000281.verbatim:
Pain Relievers — Mineral Replacement: Ca, Mg, Cu, Se:
Propoxyphene (Darvon Compound, Darvocet, Wygesic). Addictive, no more effective than aspirin, has more side effects than morphine, causes seizures and heart complications.
Pentazocine (Talwin). Addictive, no more effective than aspirin, has more side effects than morphine, causes seizures and heart complications.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000282.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists dementia treatments deemed not effective for older patients — Cyclandelate and Isoxsuprine — with the mineral replacement: gallium, germanium, selenium, calcium, oxygen, chromium, vanadium, lithium, vitamin B-1 (thiamine), and vitamin B-3 (niacin), with no sugar and no caffeine.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000282.verbatim:
Dementia Treatments — Mineral Replacement: Ga, Ge, Se, Ca, O2, Cr, Va, Li, B-1, B-3 (no sugar, no caffeine):
Cyclandelate - Not effective.
Isoxsuprine - Not effective.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000283.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists the blood thinner Dipyridamole (Persantine) as unsuitable for older patients (not shown effective except with artificial heart valves), with the mineral replacement: selenium, manganese, magnesium, vitamin E, and omega-3 oils.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000283.verbatim:
Blood Thinners — Mineral Replacement: Se, Mn, Mg, Vit E, Omega 3 Oils:
Dipyridamole (Persantine). Except in patients with artificial heart valves, not shown to be effective.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000284.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists muscle relaxants/spasm relievers unsuitable for older patients — Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril), Orphenidrine (Norflex, Norgesic), Methocarbamol (Robaxin), and Carisoprodol (Soma), causing dizziness, drowsiness, fainting and falls — with the mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, boron, and lithium.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000284.verbatim:
Muscle Relaxants, Spasm Relievers — Mineral Replacement: Ca, Mg, B, Li:
Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril) - Causes dizziness, drowsiness, fainting, falls.
Orphenidrine (Norflex, Norgesic) - Causes dizziness, drowsiness, fainting, falls.
Methocarbamol (Roboxin) - Causes dizziness, drowsiness, falls.
Carisoprodol (Soma) - Potential for nervous system toxicity is greater than potential benefit.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000285.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists the anti-nausea/anti-vomiting drug Trimethobenzamide (Tigan) as unsuitable for older patients (not very effective; causes drowsiness, dizziness and falls), with the mineral replacement: bismuth, calcium, and lithium.
WAL-CLM-RARE-000285.verbatim:
Anti-Nausea Drugs, Anti-Vomiting Drugs — Mineral Replacement: Bi, Ca, Li:
Trimethobenzamide (Tigan). Not very effective. Causes drowsiness, dizziness and falls.

WAL-CLM-RARE-000286.claim_text: Wallach's Table 9-1 lists antihypertensive drugs unsuitable for older patients — Propranolol (Inderal), Methyldopa (Aldoril, Aldomet), and Reserpine (Regroton, Hydropres), causing mental/physical slowing or depression — with the mineral replacement: calcium, magnesium, omega-3, and vitamin B-6 (pyridoxine).
WAL-CLM-RARE-000286.verbatim:
Antihypertensive — Mineral Replacement: Ca, Mg, Omega 3, B6:
Propranolol (Inderal). Feeling slowed mentally and physically.
Methyldopa (Aldoril, Aldomet). Feeling mentally and physically slowed.
Reserpine (Regroton, Hydropres). Depression.
